extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and attorneys before the USPTO; OED adjudicators; attorneys facing USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules governing the professional conduct of patent practitioners before the USPTO, especially duties to clients and candor to the Office as applied in disciplinary proceedings. Focuses on failures to communicate, neglect, conflicts of interest, and false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of a legal matter (37 C.F.R. § 10.77)
rubrics_metrics.description: By failing to respond to the Office Action, and allowing the application to become abandoned, Respondent neglected a legal matter entrusted to him, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.77.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and context in the decision: failing to file a response to non-final Office Actions, Notices to File Missing Parts, Notices to File Corrected Application Papers; allowing patent applications to go abandoned. Repeated failures across multiple applications are strong indicia of neglect. The decision treats failure to act on Office correspondence as neglect even where client did not revive the application later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to seek lawful objectives of the client (37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent failed to seek the lawful objectives of the Bartols (and other clients), in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where the practitioner did not pursue prosecution of a client’s patent application or otherwise carry out the client’s objectives (e.g., not responding to Office Actions that would further prosecution). The Board considers whether the practitioner acted consistent with client directions and whether the client consented to abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform client of Office correspondence that could have a significant effect (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a),(b) through § 10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: By failing to inform the Bartols of the Notice of Abandonment, Respondent also failed to inform a client of Office correspondence that could have a significant effect on a pending matter, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) and (b) through § 10.23(c)(8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: failing to notify clients of Notices to File Missing Parts, Notices of Abandonment, and other Office correspondence. The Board emphasizes prompt notice and recognizes practical consequences (costs of revival, shortened patent term) as evidence of prejudice. Practitioner should promptly notify clients of any Office communication that may materially affect the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional failure to carry out contract of employment; prejudice or damage to client (37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(2) and (3))
rubrics_metrics.description: By allowing the patent application to go abandoned, Respondent intentionally '[f]ail[ed] to carry out a contract of employment entered into with a client for professional services' and intentionally '[p]rejudice[d] or damage[d] a client during the course of a professional relationship,' in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(2) and (3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where the practitioner’s omissions (e.g., not prosecuting applications, not informing clients) cause financial or procedural harm (e.g., revival fees, lost patent term). The decision treats intentional or knowing failures more severely; evidence includes client testimony that they did not consent to abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate and obtain client informed consent (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: After May 3, 2013, by not informing her of the Notice to File Missing Parts and by not filing a response to it, he failed to '[p]romptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance with respect to which the client’s informed consent is required by the USPTO Rules,' failed to '[r]easonably consult with the client about the means by which the client’s objectives are to be accomplished' and failed to 'explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation,' in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(1) and (2) and 11.104(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific duties include: promptly informing clients when their informed consent is required; reasonably consulting about means to accomplish objectives; explaining matters sufficiently to permit informed decisions; keeping clients reasonably informed about status and promptly complying with reasonable requests for information (11.104(a)(3),(4)). Failure to respond to client emails or otherwise communicate can violate these provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting scope of representation requires informed consent (37 C.F.R. § 11.102(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner is allowed to limit the scope of the traditional attorney-client relationship 'if the limitation is reasonable under the circumstances and the client gives informed consent.' 37 C.F.R. § 11.102(c). Respondent did not get informed consent from Ms. __ to limit his contact with her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must obtain and document informed consent when restricting communications or otherwise narrowing representation (e.g., dealing only with a single point of contact). Absent informed consent, limiting contact with a co-client can constitute a breach of duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of loyalty and handling joint-client conflicts (fiduciary duty; case law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fiduciary relationship of an attorney creates a duty not to act contrary to, or assume a position inconsistent with, his client’s interests. Where two parties are jointly prosecuting a patent application, they are commonly considered to be joint clients; an attorney representing joint clients faces the risk of conflicting interests and must safeguard unimpaired loyalty. (Citations: Merck Eprova AG v. ProThera, Johnson v. Haberman & Kassoy.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing co-inventors/joint clients the practitioner must identify potential conflicts, obtain appropriate consents, and not favor one client over another. The decision treats failure to account for the risk of dual representation (e.g., allowing an application to be abandoned without notifying the other joint client) as a violation of professional duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality does not trump duty to co-client communication
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent that Respondent implies that maintaining Mr. __ as sole point of contact was in furtherance of an attorney’s duty to maintain confidentiality, this duty was misplaced with respect to avoiding disclosure to Ms. __. 'A lawyer’s obligation to communicate to one client all information needed to make an informed decision qualifies the [attorney’s] duty to maintain the confidentiality of a co-client’s information.' (A v. B, 158 N.J. 51.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner cannot use confidentiality as a blanket justification to withhold information from co-clients when the withheld information is necessary for the co-client to make an informed decision about the representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to seek permission to withdraw if unable to contact client
rubrics_metrics.description: If Respondent could not reach his client, he had the obligation to seek permission from the Office to withdraw representation (citing Allison v. Comm’n for Lawyer Discipline). Inability to contact a client does not relieve an attorney of his duty to the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner genuinely cannot contact a client, the appropriate step is to seek withdrawal per USPTO procedures rather than ignore office notices or allow abandonment. Failure to do so can be treated as neglect or intentional misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward a tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly: (1) make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal by the practitioner; (2) ... ; (3) offer evidence that the practitioner knows to be false. If a practitioner, the practitioner’s client, or a witness called by the practitioner, has offered material evidence and the practitioner comes to know of its falsity, the practitioner shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal. 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule corresponds to ABA Model Rule 3.3. It is aimed at avoiding conduct that undermines the integrity of the adjudicative process. Preparing or submitting statements the practitioner knows to be false to the Office or tribunal violates this rule; remedial obligations include correcting and, if necessary, disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on false statements and failure to cooperate in disciplinary matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules provide that a practitioner in connection with a disciplinary or reinstatement matter shall not: (a) knowingly make a false statement of material fact; (b) fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a misapprehension known by the person to have arisen in the matter, fail to cooperate with the Office ... in an investigation of any matter before it, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority. 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(a),(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to statements made to OED and to cooperation with investigations. Examples in the decision: preparing a statement containing falsehoods for a client to sign and failing to timely correct or disclose that the client refused to sign. Noncooperation and knowingly making false statements in disciplinary contexts have led to suspension/exclusion in precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct: dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation and prejudicial conduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c),(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to: (c) engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation; (d) engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice. 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c),(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes false statements to clients and to the Office, and conduct impeding disciplinary investigation. The Director argues such conduct is 'serious misconduct' and precedent supports significant discipline for these violations (e.g., suspension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable practitioner would confirm abandonment decisions in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A reasonable practitioner would confirm in writing such a serious matter as deciding to abandon a patent application, particularly if he had to persuade the client not to pursue it after being given written direction to pursue the application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner guidance/anti-pattern: when client gives written direction to pursue an application, any later decision to abandon should be documented in writing and, where appropriate, obtain express consent. Oral or vague recollections ('I thought I had secured the acquiescence') are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client prejudice and practical consequences must be considered (revival fees, shortened patent term)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board notes practical consequences of abandonment: the PTO petition-to-revive fee (approx. $1,600 for a large entity or $800 in other contexts), legal fees for preparing the petition, and the requirement to show the delay was unintentional; delay can also shorten patent term (35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2)), reducing value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating misconduct and damage, the Board considers the cost and procedural hurdles to revival and the potential loss in patent term as evidence of prejudice to clients. Practitioner must inform clients of these consequences when office actions or abandonment are possible.
